BACKGROUND. This is the media pipeline for a two-person video podcast. Every episode begins as four separate WebM files recorded by a Daily.co room: host camera audio, host camera video, guest camera audio, guest camera video. Each file starts whenever that device joined the call, so the four files do not share a zero. In the reference episode the host tracks start at 0.225s and 0.229s while the guest tracks start at 224.875s and 224.896s, because the guest joined 224.7 seconds late. The tracks also contain dropouts, meaning stretches where packets stopped arriving: host audio has one 76.860s hole at 151.859s, and host video has thirteen holes totalling 219.960s including a 203.887s frozen stretch starting at 25.713s.

A module was just added that handles this correctly. In server/pipeline/av_sync.py, derive_timeline() computes ONE session grid with T=0 at the earliest packet across all four tracks, measures every dropout as a packet hole, and build_stems() renders four stems that are all exactly the same length on that grid, with dropouts HELD (silence for audio, frozen frame for video) and never removed. It writes a timeline.json describing the grid, the per-track offsets onto the grid, and every hole.

THE PROBLEM YOU ARE MAPPING: nothing consumes any of that. The rest of the pipeline still re-derives its own timing from the raw WebM files. Five consecutive renders of the reference episode shipped with broken audio as a result. The work now starting will make the session grid the single coordinate system for the whole episode, with any stage that computes its own timing failing a pin check.

YOUR SURFACE: the composite stage and everything that produces or consumes sync offsets. Read at least these files in the snapshot: server/pipeline/orchestrator.py (the function _render_publishable_program begins near line 2579 and is the heart of this), server/pipeline/av_sync.py, and server/pipeline/video_assembly.py.

ANSWER THESE FIVE QUESTIONS. Anchor every claim to a file and line you actually read.
1. Every site where sync offsets are derived, and from exactly which inputs. Name the function and the line.
2. Every site where the composite video is built, and exactly which media files it reads.
3. What an offset MEANS dimensionally at each site: relative to which zero, and in which direction (does a positive value delay or advance that track). If two sites disagree about the sense of the number, say so loudly, because that is the class of bug we are hunting.
4. What specifically would have to change for the composite to read the four stems plus timeline.json instead of the raw files, and what currently depends on the existing offsets that would break when it does.
5. Any code path where a fallback, a default, an exception handler, or a cached value could silently re-enter raw-track derivation after the rewire. These are the highest value findings in this lane.

DO NOT propose a patch and do not write code. Map what exists.

OUTPUT CONTRACT: write ./report.md in your working directory. Open with a two sentence summary of the surface. Then one section per question above, numbered 1 to 5. Every finding must carry a citation in the exact form path/to/file.py:LINE, using real line numbers you read from the snapshot; invented line numbers are checked and will fail. Cite at least eight distinct locations across the report. Where you are uncertain, say so and name what you would have to run to settle it.

You must NOT modify, create, or delete any file anywhere except the single file ./report.md in your own current working directory. Do not run git. Do not commit. BACKGROUND. This is the media pipeline for a two-person video podcast. Every episode begins as four separate WebM files from a Daily.co room, one audio and one video per participant, each starting whenever that device joined, so they do not share a zero. Tracks also contain dropouts where packets stopped arriving.

FIVE RENDERS OF ONE EPISODE SHIPPED BROKEN, all of them audio, and the gates are the reason we care about each one. The five defects were:
  (a) the renderer certified the CONTAINER duration instead of counting decoded audio samples, so a file that measured correct was wrong;
  (b) an ffmpeg -shortest flag truncated the tail of the AAC program mux;
  (c) a constant-frame-rate clean INSERTED audio samples because per-contribution presentation timestamps were not rebuilt;
  (d) the gates judged audio/video divergence without first locating the A/V anchors, so they compared the wrong points;
  (e) dropouts were DELETED rather than held, which slid all later audio 77 seconds early.

A module was just added that fixes (e) at the source: server/pipeline/av_sync.py derives ONE session grid with T=0 at the earliest packet across all four tracks and renders four stems that are all the same length on that grid, holding every dropout instead of removing it. The ratified rule is now: no stage may remove time from one track without removing it from all four.

YOUR SURFACE: the gates. Read server/pipeline/media_gates.py in full, and read every place the orchestrator records or acts on a gate result in server/pipeline/orchestrator.py (search for _record_media_gate and for gate_result).

ANSWER THESE FIVE QUESTIONS. Anchor every claim to a file and line you actually read.
1. Enumerate every gate that measures anything about timing or duration. For each one: what does it measure, what does it compare that measurement against, and what tolerance does it allow?
2. Take the five defects (a) through (e) above one at a time. For each, say whether a gate as currently written WOULD have caught it, and cite the gate. Where the answer is no, say what measurement was missing. Be honest; a gate that only would have caught it by luck counts as no.
3. A master-conformance gate is planned: it will measure the rendered artifact BACK to the session grid at several probe points and fail if any speaker's audio or video has moved. Where in the current code would it hook in, and what would it need access to that it does not have today?
4. A no-time-removal gate is planned: after any cut, all four tracks must still be the same length. Where would that hook in, and is there any existing gate it would duplicate?
5. FALSE GREENS. Find every gate that can report success on a missing input, an inapplicable condition, a skipped measurement, or an exception it swallowed. Look hard at any not-applicable or waiver path. A gate that passes when it did not actually measure anything is the most dangerous thing in this file, so this section is the most important one in your report.

DO NOT propose a patch and do not write code. Map what exists.

OUTPUT CONTRACT: write ./report.md in your working directory. Open with a two sentence summary. Then one section per question above, numbered 1 to 5. Question 2 must be answered as a table with one row per defect (a) through (e). Every finding must carry a citation in the exact form path/to/file.py:LINE, using real line numbers you read from the snapshot; invented line numbers are checked and will fail. Cite at least eight distinct locations across the report. Where you are uncertain, say so and name what you would have to run to settle it.
